title: Woodwork Bench
strapline: Real tools, real wood, real pride.
intent: Real woodwork with real tools tells children they are trusted and capable, and that shows in how seriously they rise to it.
Hammering, sawing, drilling and screwing build genuine hand and arm strength, coordination and control.
Woodwork is deep problem-solving: joining, balancing and making a real idea hold together.
Managing sharp, heavy tools safely is powerful learning about risk, care and looking after yourself and others.
The pride of making a real object — a boat, a robot, a name plaque — is a huge boost to confidence and perseverance.
implementation: Set up a proper low bench with real, child-sized tools — hammer, saw, hand-drill, vice — and soft wood, golf tees and bottle tops.
Teach and insist on clear safety routines: goggles on, one person hammering at a time, wood held in the vice.
Stay close and supervise, but let children do the real work — resist taking the tool from them.
Model the language of the process: 'Hold it steady in the vice, then tap gently to start the nail.'
Talk through the problems with them: 'The two pieces won't stay together — what could hold them?'
Celebrate effort and persistence over neatness, and display what children make.
Start small and achievable — hammering tees into a pumpkin or foam — and build up as skill and confidence grow.
key_questions: What are you making — what will it need to work?
How can we keep the wood steady while you saw?
These two pieces won't stay together — what could join them?
How do we keep ourselves and our friends safe at the bench?
That was tricky — how did you keep going until it worked?

impact.text: Children hammer, saw, drill and join with growing strength, coordination and control.
Children build and construct real objects, solving how to make the parts hold together.
Children work out how things join and balance, testing and adjusting until it holds.
Children handle real tools carefully and follow the safety routines to look after themselves and others.
Children persist through the tricky bits and take real pride in what they have made.
Children talk about their plan and process using tool and joining vocabulary.

enhancements: Real child-sized tools: hammer, tenon saw, hand-drill, screwdriver, vice and safety goggles.
Soft offcuts, balsa, corks, golf tees, bottle tops and lolly sticks to join.
A pumpkin, foam block or clay for early, safe hammering practice.
Sandpaper and a finishing area for smoothing and painting the work.
Photos or simple plans of things to make — a boat, a plane, a robot.
A clear safety poster the children help to write and follow.

playing_exploring: Children take on a real, grown-up challenge with genuine tools and rise to being trusted.
They take safe risks and test what the tools and wood will do.
active_learning: Children persist through difficulty, staying with a demanding job until their idea holds together.
creating_thinking: Children plan what to make, solve how to join and balance it, and adapt when it doesn't work first time.
